This is the discussion thread for Numina Fuse. See #General announcements > Numina Fuse.

Please include any feedback or bugs here.

Applying requires installing a Github App that requires the permission "Know which resources you can access".

Is this necessary? In my understanding this leaks the names of all private repositories to which I have access to Numina.

@Kim Morrison If you choose "Only select repositories" (which is what we strongly recommend to any users of Fuse), then, by extension of only being able to access those repositories, we can only see the names of those repositories. Indeed, upon further evaluation, I can confirm Fuse can only see the five (5) repositories that I have selected. Please let us know if you have any evidence to the contrary.
I accepted anyway, despite my misgivings above, but I don't recall seeing any "only select repositories" option in the dialog.

There are two GitHub steps involved:

(a) User authorization: this is the initial GitHub sign-in / consent screen. This is where GitHub shows "Know which resources you can access." In Fuse, this is used to identify you and get a GitHub user token; we do not request broad OAuth scopes here.

(b) GitHub App installation: this is the step where you grant the GitHub App access to repositories. This is where GitHub lets you choose "All repositories" or "Only select repositories." We strongly recommend choosing "Only select repositories."

The important point is that the warning in (a) does not by itself give Fuse access to all private repositories you can access. Per GitHub model, the app can determine resources you can access that the app can also access. For private repositories, Fuse access is bounded by the GitHub App installation in (b), i.e. the repositories selected during installation.
To what extent is Numina Fuse open source?
Fuse is closed source right now. We would have to discuss internally what we can open source. In the past, Project Numina has extensively open sourced its research and work.

Hi, thank you for giving me access to Numia Fuse. I’ve spent a few hours exploring it, and here are my thoughts.

Previously, I had an idea for a platform like this. It would be amazing if there were a tool similar to Overleaf, where you could write math content in LaTeX, hit the compile button, and not only generate a PDF but also produce the corresponding Lean code and compile it to immediately verify whether your math is correct. This would allow people with limited experience in Lean or formalization to benefit as well. I would say that Numia Fuse makes this idea a reality, at least to some extent.

So far, I haven’t encountered any serious bugs during my use, but I have two minor user interface suggestions:

  1. At the beginning, Fuse asks you to start by writing or uploading a blueprint. This is not very convenient. A better approach would be for the agent to generate the blueprint automatically based on the existing Lean files in the repository or any provided LaTeX files containing math content.
  2. Once the blueprint and its dependency relationships are clear, it should be easy to generate a dependency graph. Visualization can be very helpful, especially for a platform like this. I hope you can add a dependency graph feature in the future.

Hi @Jinzheng Li, thanks for the feedback.

The goal is to have the user write down the source text at the beginning (not a blueprint). This is supposed to be the math you want to formalize. We then generate a blueprint from it using the math already in Mathlib and your repository. Are you wanting to write the source text with the AI in the editor as well?

Adding a dependency graph would not be too hard. Our main concern was that we want to do large scale formalizations where a dependency graph may not be too convenient. However, seeing that people do indeed want this feature, we will take that into consideration.

It seems like there a few more easy to integrate features that people would like in Fuse.

(1) A sorry mode, that simply looks at existing repository with sorrys and then launches prover agents to fill those sorrys.

(2) The ability to work on (or on top of) existing branches. (done!)

(3) Being able to select or work with existing blueprints. (done!)

We are looking forward to hearing more ideas, so we can do our best to develop them.

@Jinzheng Li We added the a "Graph" tab to the blueprint viewer to visualize the dependencies.

Please let us know if you have any other suggestions.

@Justin Asher

Thanks for the quick update! The "Graph" looks great, just as I expected. I’m currently trying to tackle some graduate-level problems using Numina Fuse. The prover in Numina Fuse works really well. Is this just the numina-lean-agent, or have you made significant improvements beyond that?

Based on my experience so far, the feature I’d find most useful right now is a "hyperlink" function. When reading Lean code, hyperlinks could take me directly to the corresponding declaration in Blueprint, and vice versa. It would also be great to use these links in the "Graph" to navigate quickly between Blueprint and Lean code.

This was an original feature in Blueprint, which I found extremely helpful. There’s a similar feature in Overleaf, which makes me think it’s an important functionality to include.
@Jinzheng Li We will take this suggestion into consideration.

Fuse now has the ability to work with existing blueprints:

As an example, I plugged in @Kevin Buzzard's FLT blueprint:

More to come!

Note that this is different from starting from an informal source, where we create a lightweight "blueprint" in a Numina folder. This is meant to work with existing blueprints in the sense of @Patrick Massot's leanblueprint repository.

We have updated our commit system to add a few new features:

(1) A Git tab that enables you to see the Git history for the current branch along with any pending changes:

(2) The ability to turn on and off automatic commits, meaning you either let the AI control when to commit or you do so yourself:

(3) AI generated commit titles and descriptions. Before, they were being mechanically generated, and cluttering the Git history. Now, they are selectively generated and properly titled.

What is the suggested/preferred prescription for axioms?

I'm formalizing Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (AQFT), which is an axiomatic framework for quantum field theory. Thus I require axioms. So I have a blueprint with entries of the form

\begin{axiom}[Local Algebras]
    \label{axm:local-algebras}
    \uses{def:alexandrov-topology}
    \uses{def:minkowski-spacetime}
    \uses{def:chronological-future-and-chronological-past}
    For any basis element $\mathbf{B}$ of the Alexandrov topology on Minkowski spacetime, i.e. any set of the form $I^+(p) \cap I^-(q)$, there is a corresponding abstract C*-algebra $\mathfrak{U}(\mathbf{B})$
    \begin{align}
        \mathbf{B} \longmapsto \mathfrak{U}(\mathbf{B}),
    \end{align}
    and when $\mathbf{B}$ is the empty set, we have the distinguished correspondence
    \begin{align}
        \emptyset \longmapsto \mathbb{C} \mathbf{1},
    \end{align}
    where $\mathbf{1}$ is the multiplicative identity in the abstract C*-algebra $\mathbb{C} \mathbf{1}$.
\end{axiom}

which currently seem to be ignored, e.g. they do not appear in the graphical representation of the dependencies.

What is the suggested/preferred prescription to handle such axioms?
Thanks for pointing this out—yes, we need to add other types of data to be displayed properly. I will add an issue for this and fix it ASAP. Please let me know if you run into any other issues.

@Kelly Davis, I think it's not a good idea to say "thus I require axioms". Axioms are never needed in Lean. :-) You can always just write conditional theorems, which take additional hypotheses. I highly recommend that everyone does this, and never ever uses Lean's axiom keyword...
@Kim Morrison As an example, how would you suggest to modify the provided example to use a theorem environment and not an axiom environment?

Replace

axiom foo : False
theorem p : P := False.elim foo

with

theorem p : False -> P := False.elim

As to your example above, you should just be defining a structure for an AQFT, with fields for the "axioms".

One could say that you need "axioms" to define a ring, but ...

@Kim Morrison My question was more on the LaTeX/Numina Fuse side, that's why I was referring to LaTeX "environments". (Sorry if that wasn't clear.)

Once things are in Lean something like what you suggested can work. The question is more how to get an "axiom" into Lean using Numina Fuse.

@Kelly Davis The Claude error is fixed.

In case anyone else has this problem...I just decided to ask the system what I should do about the original "axiom problem", because why not.

It suggested re-writing the axioms as definitions, then bundling the definitions in an enclosing def:haag-kastler-net that \uses all the axiom-as-definitions. This would allow use something like

theorem exists_cstar_of_basis (N : HaagKastlerNet) (B : AlexandrovBasis 𝕄) :
    ∃ A : CStarAlgebra ℂ, A = N.U B := ⟨N.U B, rfl⟩

I'll see how it goes letting the system make minor mods (other than the standard additions of \leanfile, \leanok, and the like) to my blueprint.

We shipped a batch of updates to Fuse, our tool for formalizing proofs in Lean 4. New features:

  • The blueprint and formalizer agents now call reviewer agents in an iterative pipeline, so drafted blueprints get broken into pieces small enough to often be formalized and proved. (The formalization refinement still needs work.)
  • The prover agents now use DeepSeek V4 Flash, which allows users to prove more declarations by bringing down costs.
  • Provers run in a semaphore of 8 at a time, so you can queue up dozens or more declarations at once and watch them get worked through.
  • Auto mode now shows what the agents are working on live, instead of hiding it behind an "auto mode is running" screen.
  • You can see your active running sessions in the navbar.

Next we hope to let the agents run longer and produce higher quality proofs and formalizations.

I have been using the new version to formalize lean-eval problems and found it much more pleasant. Often I would leave for an hour and come back to a few thousand lines of complete Lean code.

Kelly Davis said:

What is the suggested/preferred prescription to handle such axioms?

Fuse should parse axioms now (whenever the fix deploys to production) along with a few other standard environments (theorem, lemma, corollary, definition, proposition, axiom, conjecture, example, remark, hypothesis, claim, assumption, notation).

Here are some new features that we shipped to Fuse:

  • Standard leanblueprint structure: New and AI-drafted blueprints use a table-of-contents entrypoint that \inputs per-topic chapter files under chapters/, instead of one big file. The writer keeps chapters reasonably sized and the reviewer flags bloated ones.
  • Repository source library: Upload or hand-write multiple sources (PDF, LaTeX, or Markdown), see them listed in a Sources panel, scope each to the whole repo or a specific project/blueprint, and delete them individually. The AI can read and search across several when drafting.
  • Explorer agent: A new read-only explorer agent searches Mathlib, your project's dependencies, and the repo itself for existing declarations before formalizing, so the AI reuses what's already proved instead of re-deriving it.
  • Formalization status via \leanok: Fuse reads \leanok tags to show per-declaration progress and writes them back when a declaration is formalized/proved, so status lives in the source and shows up in git/PRs (existing markers in an imported blueprint are respected).
  • One floating section selector: Navigating a multi-file blueprint is unified into a single selector (bottom-right), consistent across overview, graph, and editor views.
  • Multi-Lean-project repositories: Repos with several Lean projects in subfolders now work instead of being hidden as "no lakefile." New Blueprint shows a project picker (auto-selected when there's just one), and New Project can target a subdirectory and open a PR adding the lakefile/toolchain/starter module.
